Finally, note that an ns orbital has n 2 1 ­radial nodes; a radial node is a spheri- cal surface about the nucleus on which c and c2 are 0. These spherical surfaces are the analogues of the nodal planes in the wave functions for a particle in a cubic box (Figure 4.31). The more numerous the nodes in an orbital, the higher the energy of the corresponding quantum state of the atom. Just as for the particle in a box, the energies of orbitals increase as the number of nodes increases.

The angular wave function Y10( ) , with the combination , 5 1, m 5 0 is called the angular portion of the pz orbital here because it is oriented along the z-axis. The wave function Ypz for the pz orbital (see Table 5.2) is proportional to cos u. From the relation between spherical and Cartesian coordinates illustrated in Figure 5.1, you can see that cos u } z; thus, this orbital has its maximum amplitude along the z-axis (where u 5 0 or p) and a node in the x-y plane (where = >2, so cos u 5 0) (Fig. 5.9a). The pz orbital therefore points along the z-axis, with its positive phase (red in Fig. 5.9a) on the side of the x-y plane where the z-axis is posi- tive and negative phase (blue in Fig. 5.9a) on the side where the z-axis is negative. The positive and negative lobes are circles tangent to one another at the x-y plane. An electron in a pz orbital has the greatest probability of being found at significant values of z and has zero probability of being found in the x-y plane. This plane is a nodal plane or, more generally, an ­angular node across which the wave function changes sign.
